summary.text: A 76-year-old man with diabetes mellitus (erratic control), hypertension and ischemic heart disease presented with two weeks of intermittent fever and productive cough with yellowish sputum, without hemoptysis, significant weight loss or TB history/contact.
On examination he was febrile but hemodynamically stable (SpO2 98% on room air, BP 130/80 mmHg, pulse 110 bpm) with bilateral coarse crepitations and no respiratory distress.

Workup showed neutrophilic leukocytosis with markedly elevated inflammatory markers, bilateral nodular shadows on chest radiograph and tree-in-bud nodules with peribronchial consolidation on HRCT in keeping with invasive fungal pneumonia; sputum grew coliforms and was TB-culture negative.

Bronchoscopy BAL galactomannan was highly positive (7.92), BAL fungal culture isolated Aspergillus fumigatus and BAL TB testing was negative, establishing microbiologically confirmed pulmonary aspergillosis.

Ceftriaxone with clarithromycin gave minimal improvement at 48 hours and was escalated to renal-adjusted meropenem for 14 days with a suboptimal response; he then received intravenous liposomal amphotericin 200 mg daily for 10 days (initial elevated transaminases and impaired renal function) until transaminases normalized, then oral voriconazole 200 mg bd.

He improved remarkably with antifungal therapy and his fever resolved; the discussion reports favorable clinical, biochemical and radiological outcomes. The discussion statement that voriconazole was withheld for drug-induced hepatitis in all three cases conflicts with his narrative.

summary.text: A 43-year-old man with diabetes and poor glycemic control presented with three weeks of intermittent fever, constitutional symptoms and productive cough, without hemoptysis on admission or known TB contact; he was febrile with left upper zone coarse crepitations and bronchial breathing.
Blood tests showed neutrophilic leukocytosis and markedly elevated inflammatory markers (Table 1 values retained), and sputum screening for pyogenic organisms, TB and fungi was negative.

Empirical piperacillin-tazobactam for 10 days gave minimal improvement; an antituberculosis fixed-dose regimen was started on clinical suspicion of tuberculosis and bronchoscopy with BAL sampling was done.

In hospital he developed acute shortness of breath then hemoptysis; chest X-ray showed a left hydropneumothorax treated with an intercostal tube (hemorrhagic drainage), and HRCT showed an encysted left hydropneumothorax with left upper lobe ground glass/cavitating consolidation and right upper-predominant patchy consolidations.
BAL fungal culture isolated Aspergillus species, confirming pulmonary aspergillosis.

Voriconazole 200 mg twice daily was switched to liposomal amphotericin 200 mg daily after three days because of deranged liver biochemistry; he deteriorated to respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation and died on the second ICU day.

summary.text: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease and ischemic heart disease post-CABG, transferred from a local hospital, had two weeks of fever with chills and rigors and productive cough with rusty-colored sputum.

He was febrile, ill-looking but hemodynamically stable (SpO2 96%, BP 140/90 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm) with bilateral coarse crepitations and occasional rhonchi; laboratory work showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, markedly elevated inflammatory markers and deranged baseline renal and liver biochemistry, with COVID-19 reported negative.
Chest radiograph and HRCT showed bilateral cavitating lesions with internal air loculi, patchy ground glass and peribronchial thickening, suggestive of necrotizing pneumonia.

Sputum grew Candida albicans and bronchial wash grew Pseudomonas species; TB, autoimmune, melioidosis and blood culture tests were negative and echocardiography did not suggest infective endocarditis; BAL galactomannan was positive (2.41) and BAL fungal culture isolated Aspergillus fumigatus, confirming pulmonary aspergillosis.

He received meropenem and intravenous voriconazole (maintenance given nine days before transfer, then withheld for worsening liver function), then liposomal amphotericin B for 10 days with renal, electrolyte and liver monitoring.

He improved clinically and radiologically; repeat serum Aspergillus IgG was negative at 40 days (BAL galactomannan 0.53 was reported with it as negative) and follow-up HRCT showed significant interval resolution.

article_limitations: Three-patient case series from one Sri Lankan tertiary respiratory center; reported count of three individual patients matches the three Case sections; no cited cases from the reference list are assigned to patients.

Table 1 prints hemoglobin as mg/dl and CRP as mg/dL (reference <6) and count units as ×10^(9)/L; values and units are retained verbatim without conversion, flags or diagnoses derived from reference ranges. Table 1 has no stated sample timing.

Galactomannan source inconsistencies: Case 1 narrative says sputum galactomannan positive while Table 1 lists serum 2.02; Case 3 Table 1 serum galactomannan is a dash while the discussion cites a positive serum galactomannan for Cases 1 and 3; Case 3 repeat BAL galactomannan 0.53 is called negative despite a printed reference <0.5. Conflicting statements are review-only.

Discussion claims voriconazole was withheld for drug-induced hepatitis in all three cases; this conflicts with the Case 1 narrative (amphotericin first, then oral voriconazole) and is review-only for Case 1.

Case 2 BAL TB study result and outcome of the antituberculosis regimen are not reported; Case 2 and 3 timing relative to ICU admission, transfer and bronchoscopy is only partly stated. No discharge dates or long-term follow-up are given for Cases 1 and 3, and no dates appear anywhere in the article.
